claim: A delay's damping byte is one pole, and it is the pole written the cheapest way there is: a running average, one multiply and one state, with no zero at half the rate. That is not the section the same part's chorus filter byte sits on. A pole put through the bilinear transform keeps a zero at half the rate and its skirt bends steeper as it climbs towards it; this one has no zero, so its skirt stops cutting and levels off -- and the profile does level off, on every one of the ten settings the run asked, at a different depth each time. Where a profile levels off names the pole outright with nothing fitted, because the depth is one minus the coefficient over one plus it. Scored through the same takes the cheap pole is sixteen times the bilinear one's median and is the only candidate of eight whose residual does not lean. And it names the clock a fourth time, by a route none of the first three used: the coefficient that puts the corner where the page prints it depends on the rate, so a corner fitted freely from each setting's own skirt lands on the printed third octaves to a five-hundredth of an octave at thirty-two kilohertz and a twentieth at forty-four -- high at every setting, which is a lean and not a scatter.
named: a one-multiply pole, the running average a fixed-point part damps a delay's repeats with

document_rows.why: Which byte this is and what the page prints against it. The range is what the corners are held against and the Bypass is what the run took its flat reference at; neither is evidence about a section, and the section is read off the shape of the skirt. The feedback row is here because it is the reason this byte exists and the reason the run held it at its centre.

era_priors.claim: A pole written as a running average costs one multiply and one state; put through the bilinear transform it costs two multiplies and a sample of the input kept beside the sample of the output. What the cheap one gives up is the zero at half the rate, which is a defect in a filter meant to shape a signal and nothing at all in one meant to take the top off a delay's repeats.
era_priors.why: It says why one part would hold both forms rather than one, which is what the two records together show and what the class's own prior argued against. The prior that a section is written once and reached from more than one byte holds inside a type here and not across the part.
era_priors.would_be_wrong_if: This byte's skirt had gone on cutting past the corner instead of levelling off, or the chorus's filter byte had levelled off too. Both were measured and each record puts the other's section twelve to sixteen decibels out, so the prior is being carried by a difference rather than by a habit.

adds: The record says what this byte did to each twelfth-octave band at ten settings, and carries the steepest slope each was running at. What is read out of it here is that the section is one pole, that the pole is written without the bilinear transform's zero, that this is not the section another type's filter byte sits on, and that the rate the coefficient implies is thirty-two kilohertz. The record names no section, no coefficient and no clock, and says so.

what_the_corner_table_is.what: Not this claim's, and cited rather than fitted. Where these corners are is the frequency class's and is closed. What is done with them here is the other way round: each candidate fits its own corner freely from one setting's own skirt, and the printed series is then used to ask which candidate's corners landed on it. A section written the wrong way has no reason to put a freely fitted corner on a series nobody handed the fitter.
what_the_corner_table_is.which_read_the_same_range_another_way: That claim read this range off the profiles directly and put its entries a median 0.0053 octaves from the printed series. This fit, through a section rather than through a crossing, puts them a median 0.0022. Two readings of one table by two methods agreeing to a few thousandths of an octave is what says the section and the table are both right, since a wrong section would have had to be wrong in a way that happened to land on the other reading.

alternatives.reading: The same cheap pole clocked at the converter's rate rather than the part's.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: Where its corners land. The coefficient that puts a corner at a given frequency depends on the rate, so a corner fitted freely to each setting's skirt and then held against the third octaves the page prints is a reading of the rate. At thirty-two the ten settings land a median 0.0022 octaves from the series with no sign to them; at forty-four they land a median 0.0548 away and every one of the ten is high, growing from 0.042 octaves at the bottom entry to 0.087 near the top. That is a lean in a quantity the other reading of this same range resolves to about five thousandths of an octave.

alternatives.reading: The section is the bilinear pole the chorus's filter byte sits on, and what levels off at the top of the band is the chain's own floor rather than the section.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: The bands where the floor is were taken out before any candidate saw the record, on the record's own admission rule -- a band is scored only where every setting's reading stands ten decibels over the same chain's silence in it, which drops 2 of 113. The bilinear pole is still 11.69 dB out at its worst on what is left, and its freely fitted corners land a median 0.4677 octaves from the printed series -- a third of an octave and more, high at every setting. A floor does not move a corner.

alternatives.reading: Two of the cheap poles cascaded rather than one, which would level off twice as deep.
alternatives.ruled_out_by: The skirt, which the reading resolves several times over. Two poles run at twelve decibels an octave where the record's own steepest figures are between two and six, and scored through the same takes the pair is 0.445 against the winner's 0.03 and leans.

alternatives.reading: The damping sits inside the delay's own feedback loop rather than once on the way out of it.

separated_by.observable: The same sweep with the feedback byte away from its centre. The run held feedback at the middle of its printed range, which is no feedback at all, so every repeat but the first is absent and the two places the filter could sit render identically. Turn the feedback up and they stop being the same: a filter inside the loop is applied once per repeat and its cut compounds, so the tail of a held note goes on darkening, while a filter outside the loop cuts every repeat by the same amount and the tail keeps its colour.

predicts.inside the loop: the profile of the late tail cut by as many helpings of this section as there have been repeats
predicts.outside the loop: the profile of the late tail cut by exactly one, the same as the first repeat

separated_by.sensitivity_here: The section cuts up to 30 dB at its lowest setting, so two helpings against one is tens of decibels at the top of the band against the 1.40 dB the run's own repeats spread at their worst band.

run.why_this_held_block: The run's own, with two things moved. The feedback byte goes above its centre so that there are repeats to compound over, and the delay times go up from the two and a half milliseconds this run used to something long enough that the repeats can be read apart in time -- which is what lets the late tail be windowed separately from the first arrival.
run.why_a_window_and_not_a_profile: The whole take's band profile is the sum of every repeat and says little; what separates the two readings is how the profile changes from the first repeat to the last, so the stage has to be read over two windows of one take rather than over the take.

compared_against.generated_from: data/units/roland-sc8850-01/index.json, every efx-bands record filed under type 01 50 at address 40 03 0A at the twelfth-octave resolution

reproduces.how_the_model_is_read: Rendered through the very takes the record was read from and then measured on the same band set, with the chain's own silence added back where the model cuts below it -- and with the bands no reading stands ten decibels over that silence in taken out before any candidate saw the record. That last is not a convenience. The deepest settings of this byte arrive at the floor somewhere above ten kilohertz and stop falling, and a section clocked faster has a shallower skirt up there, so a reading that kept those bands would hand the rate to whichever candidate best imitated a profile that had stopped being a profile.

gross.why: median 0.03 dB against the 30.5 dB this byte commands, and a worst band of 0.87 dB -- under the 1.4 dB the run's own repeats spread at their worst band, and at the bottom of the band set rather than anywhere the section is doing something.

properties.why: Two properties, and neither is the residual. The skirt is one pole's: the record's own steepest figures run from 5.80 decibels an octave at the bottom setting to 2.27 at the top, where a second pole would put twelve. And the corners this candidate fits freely, one per setting from that setting's own skirt, land on the third octaves the page prints against this address -- 315, 400, 500, 630, 800, 1250, 2000, 3150, 5000 and 8000 -- a median 0.0022 octaves away and a worst of 0.0049. No candidate is handed that series, and the losing ones do not land on it.

power.how: contradicted on the shape and on where the corners land
power.why: Every other candidate in the class was scored on this record and every one of them leans. The bilinear pole at the same rate is the worst of the single-pole readings here, which is the reverse of how it came out on the chorus's filter byte -- the two records each put the other's section twelve to sixteen decibels out, so what separates them is not a preference but a contradiction. The two-pole and resonant-pair candidates lose on the skirt, which is what they lost on there too.

breakdown.why: the signed median swings 0.04 dB across the settings and 0.75 dB across the readings within one, against the run's own floor of 1.4 dB
breakdown.read_as: The only candidate of the eight that comes back without structure. Its worst band is at 30 Hz, which is the bottom of the band set and three decades under anything this byte moves, and it is under the run's own floor there.

refuted_by: A setting of this byte whose skirt went on cutting past its corner instead of levelling off, which would put the bilinear zero back. Or the depth it levels off at failing to follow the corner the page prints, which is the one thing about this section that is fixed rather than fitted. Or the same sweep on another type's damping byte coming back bilinear, which would make the section this slot's rather than the part's damping routine.
what_this_does_not_settle: Whether the damping sits inside the delay's feedback loop. The run held the feedback at the middle of its printed range, which is none, so there is one repeat and the two places render the same. The run that would tell them apart is in the alternatives.

Whether the other fourteen slots that print this range answer the same way. Every one of them is a delay's or a reverb's damping, which is what makes one routine the thing to expect -- but expecting is not measuring, and one slot was read.

What the coefficient's own quantum is. The corners land on the printed series to a few thousandths of an octave, which bounds the stored number from above but does not say what grid it sits on; that is the kind of question the level class answered with a scan over denominators and this reading has ten points rather than a hundred and twenty-eight.

Whether the part's high-pass damping, if it has one, is written the same way. Only the low side was swept here, and the cheap pole's high side is its own complement rather than a second routine -- which is a thing to check and not a thing to assume.
